title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment that evaluated whether a deterministic verifier pipeline (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered unique tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) a guarded pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), producing one LLM generation per task shared across arms (model_calls_used = 200; preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; failed_episode_count = 0). Observed (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0). Estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that a verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this run. The paper’s principal outcome is methodological and artifact‑grounded: we (1) publish a complete preregistered paired run and analysis, (2) explain how generation semantics and model‑call budgeting determine testability, and (3) provide concrete, archive‑grounded recommendations for reproducible repeats with independent per‑arm generation and stronger adversarial coverage. All execution and analysis artifacts cited in this paper are archived (see execution/* and analysis/* paths in the manuscript bundle).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises to reduce operator effort in NetOps but raises safety and correctness concerns: an incorrect or ill‑timed change can break reachability, violate security policies, or cause outages. Prior work proposes augmenting LLMs with deterministic validators, sandboxed replay, and generate–validate–repair loops to reduce constraint violations and hallucinations. To move beyond feasibility demonstrations we preregistered a paired confirmatory experiment (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1) that asks: How does deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic verifier → optional repair) change the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe proposals produced by a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial prompts? Our contributions are primarily methodological and reproducibility‑oriented: (1) a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment comparing an LLM baseline and a verifier‑augmented pipeline on N=200 synthetic NetOps tasks; (2) a precise artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the preregistered causal test was non‑informative in this execution; and (3) concrete, artifact‑anchored recommendations (generation semantics, adversarial budgeting, model‑call accounting) to produce an informative repeat. All inputs, raw outputs, and analyses are archived in the execution and analysis artifacts referenced throughout (e.g., execution/model_configuration.json, execution/execution_manifest.json, execution/raw_results.jsonl, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv).
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and prototype reports document growing use of LLMs in NetOps for intent translation, configuration synthesis, and limited self‑healing, and they advocate tool‑grounding and verifier‑in‑the‑loop architectures to improve correctness and reduce hallucination risk [arXiv:2605.12729; SSRN:7132138; IEEE OJCOMS 2026]. Generate–validate–repair and divide–verify–refine pipelines have been shown to reduce constraint violations in controlled settings, but reported effect sizes depend on verifier fidelity, prompt design, and generation semantics. Red‑teaming and guardrail literature emphasize trade‑offs between safety and utility (false refusals) and recommend workflow‑centred, sandboxed evaluation. Our study follows those prescriptions by (a) preregistering a paired design with explicit generation semantics, (b) deterministically generating synthetic tasks, and (c) running a deterministic sandboxed validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) with archived validator traces. Unlike prior prototype demonstrations, we (i) freeze a confirmatory estimand before execution, (ii) publish complete raw model outputs and validator traces, and (iii) explicate how execution semantics control testability.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: The preregistration (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1) defined the primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (guarded minus baseline; SAFE encoded as 1) and specified a paired binary design with N=200 unique tasks and paired episodes (planned_episode_count = 400). Sampling and task generation: a deterministic generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks under a fixed RNG seed (seed = 42) and constrained scope to single‑AS, multi‑device topologies and three configuration fields (admin, mtu, vlan). Task payloads and expected final states are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl for reproducibility. Model and generation semantics: the declared model was gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json). The preregistration allowed two generation semantics modes: independent per‑arm generations or shared_initial_candidate mode; the executed run used independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate), so a single LLM candidate was generated per task and that same candidate was scored under both baseline and guarded pipelines. Model‑call accounting: preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400 (to support independent per‑arm generation), but the execution recorded model_calls_used = 200 (execution/execution_manifest.json), consistent with shared_initial_candidate semantics (one generation per task). Validator, scoring, and labels: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed deterministic sandboxed intent/constraint validation using scoring_rule = full_intent_constraint_validation. The validator produced a binary SAFE/UNSAFE label plus deterministic validator_traces (validation_before/after, violation lists) archived per episode under execution/scoring/*.json. Repair: preregistered repair was allowed for guarded pipeline (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1) but in the confirmatory episodes no repairs were applied (repair_provider_trace = null in scoring JSONs). Analysis plan: paired_binary_analysis_v1 computed the paired contingency table, applied an exact McNemar two‑sided test (alpha = 0.05; Bonferroni adjustment planned if multiple conditions were reported), and computed a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Missingness and exclusions: preregistered deterministic duplication detection and verifier nondeterminism replacement rules were in place; execution/execution_manifest.json records completed_episode_count = 400 and failed_episode_count = 0, and analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pair_count = 200.
sections.results: Confirmatory results (adversarial cluster, per preregistration): baseline SAFE successes = 200/200; guarded SAFE successes = 200/200. The paired contingency (SAFE encoding) is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). The paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729; analysis artifacts archived). Execution accounting: planned episodes = 400 (200 tasks × 2 pipelines), completed_episode_count = 400, model_calls_used = 200, failed_episode_count = 0 (execution/execution_manifest.json). No verifier refusals or repairs occurred in the confirmatory dataset; repair_provider_trace entries are null in execution/scoring/*.json for the sampled confirmatory episodes. Representative per‑task artifacts (execution/responses/task-00000X-*.txt and execution/scoring/task-00000X-*.json) show identical shared_initial_candidate content across baseline and guarded arms for every inspected example, consistent with shared_initial_candidate execution semantics. Sensitivity and exploratory diagnostics: per the preregistration, exploratory runs reserved for verifier ROC and refusal characterization were available but were not included in the confirmatory test; analysis/contamination_summary.csv and analysis/missingness_summary.csv record zero flagged or excluded confirmatory pairs.
sections.discussion: Methodological diagnosis: three execution choices combined to make the preregistered causal test non‑informative. First, generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), so each pair received an identical LLM candidate. Second, the sampled tasks and adversarial templates, as realized against gpt‑5‑mini, produced valid candidates that passed the deterministic validator; observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%. Third, model_call budgeting (model_calls_used = 200 vs preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400) reflects the shared‑generation mode and removed the experimental degree of freedom needed for independent per‑arm variability. Together these created a ceiling effect: with identical per‑pair generations and zero baseline violations, no paired discordance could be observed and the McNemar test had no power to detect a verifier benefit. Evidence mapping: (a) execution/model_configuration.json records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and independent_condition_generation = false; (b) execution/execution_manifest.json records model_calls_used = 200, completed_episode_count = 400; (c) analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv record n11 = 200 and SAFE rates = 1.0; (d) execution/scoring/*.json contain validator_traces showing zero violations. These artifacts jointly support the non‑informative diagnosis. Recommendations for informative repeats (artifact‑anchored): (1) Use independent per‑arm generation so baseline and guarded pipelines receive distinct LLM candidates; for our N=200 design this requires allocating model_calls ≈ preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400 (one independent generation per arm per task). (2) Increase adversarial strength via templated obfuscation transforms (negation, implication, shelling of constraints) and reserve a calibrated fraction of tasks for injected unsafe candidates to exercise the verifier ROC. (3) Budget exploratory ROC/resolution runs (preregistered exploratory reserve up to 50 tasks) and report verifier true‑positive and false‑positive rates with confidence intervals. (4) Consider a small multi‑model panel to evaluate generality across model families. Operational implication: deterministic validators remain an operationally attractive guardrail, but demonstrating empirical benefit requires designing evaluation conditions that yield nonzero baseline error rates and per‑arm output variability.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived, preregistered paired experiment comparing an LLM baseline and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and for gpt‑5‑mini, both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; p = 1.0). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. The main scientific contribution is methodological: (1) preregistration choices (generation semantics, adversarial strength, and model‑call budgeting) determine whether a verifier effect is observable; (2) we publish the complete archived bundle (execution/*, analysis/*, scoring JSONs) to enable reproducible repeats; and (3) we provide artifact‑grounded, actionable recommendations for designing an informative repeat (independent per‑arm generation, increased adversarial coverage, explicit model_call budgeting). The archived artifacts cited in this paper permit exact deterministic replays of the run and serve as a concrete infrastructure template for future workflow‑centred NetOps evaluations.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in sandboxed synthetic states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
